**The lasso** addresses instability in linear regression models by penalizing larger coefficient values. See (link) for a conceptual introduction. 

In this post, we'll obtain a lasso model for `solubility` in chemical compounds using data from the `AppliedPredictiveModeling` package, which supports the excellent book of the same name. We'll do this from the machine learning perspective using the `tidymodels` framework. If you haven't worked with `tidymodels` before, I recommend pausing to check out my tutorial [here](https://youtu.be/fRj8dr-aSsU).

The `solubility` data has already been split into training and testing sets, but in each case the explanatory and response variables have been stored separately. We start by resolving this.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidymodels)
library(eeplot) # local package with personal plot theming

library(AppliedPredictiveModeling)
data(solubility)

sol_train <- solTrainXtrans |> 
  mutate(solubility = solTrainY)
sol_test <- solTestXtrans |> 
  mutate(solubility = solTestY)
```

The training set includes 951 observations while the test test includes 316. There are 228 total predictors available as we attempt to model the response variable, `solubility`.

Penalized regression in R is typically carried out using the `glmnet()` engine. Since we're using `tidymodels`, we'll rely on the `linear_reg()` wrapper, which standardizes the syntax of modeling functions like `glmnnet()` and ensures their output is compatible with the tools we'll use for tuning and evaluation. 

```{r}
my_lasso <- linear_reg(
  engine = "glmnet",
  mixture = 1, # one for lasso, zero for ridge
  penalty = tune() # lambda TBD
  ) 
```

Since there are no missing values in these sets and the variables are all numeric, little preprocessing needs to be done with this data. The following recipe (which standardizes all predictors and removes ones with zero-variance) is added for consistency and clarity.

```{r}
my_rec <- recipe(solubility ~., data = sol_train) |> 
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |> 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

my_wf <- workflow(
  spec = my_lasso,
  preprocessor = my_rec
  )
```

Since the `glmnet()` engine performs standardization by default, `step_normalize()` turns out to be redundant here. 

As a reminder, `tidymodels` separates model specification (accomplished here with `linear_reg()`) from model fitting (which we'll do later). This allows us to incorporate preprocessing in a programmatic way, via a `recipe`, ensuring our steps will be applied consistently whether we're working with the training set, the testing set, or something else entirely.

We determine the best choice for the penalty $\lambda$ using cross validation.

```{r}
# create 10-fold split
folds <- vfold_cv(
  sol_train,
  v = 10,
  repeats = 5
  ) 

# tune using a default grid of values
tune_results <- tune_grid(
  my_wf, 
  folds
  ) 

# plot results
rmse_path <- collect_metrics(tune_results) |> 
  filter(.metric == "rmse")

ggplot(rmse_path, aes(x = penalty, 
                      y = mean)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line()+
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Penalty", 
       y = "Test error") +
  theme_ee()
```

We can zoom in on the apparent minimum by specifying a data frame of penalty values for `tune_grid()` to work with. This can also be done using functions from the `dials` package, but for me this is usually more trouble than it's worth.

```{r}
my_grid <- data.frame(
  penalty = 10^seq(-4, -1, length.out = 20)
  )

tune_results <- tune_grid(
  my_wf, 
  folds, 
  grid = my_grid
  )

rmse_path <- collect_metrics(tune_results) |> 
  filter(.metric == "rmse")

ggplot(rmse_path, aes(x = penalty,
                      y = mean)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  labs(x = "Penalty",
       y = "Test error") +
  theme_ee()
```

Use `show_best()` to obtain a data frame of the best-performing hyperparameter values. Here we use root mean squared error to measure "best."

```{r}
show_best(tune_results, metric = "rmse")
```

Once we're satisfied that we've found a good hyperparameter value, we can finalize our workflow. 

```{r}
# manual specification (less common)
my_wf_final <- my_wf |> finalize_workflow(
  parameters = list(penalty = .00546)
  ) 

# automated specification (more common)
best_lambda <- select_best(tune_results, metric = "rmse")
my_wf_final <- my_wf |> finalize_workflow(best_lambda)
my_wf_final
```

A workflow is just a set of instructions. To incorporate the training data and create an algorithm for making predictions, use `fit()`. To obtain model coefficients in a tibble, use `broom::tidy()`.

```{r}
#| message: false

my_wf_fit <- my_wf_final |> 
  fit(data = sol_train)

tidy(my_wf_fit)
```

While `predict()` works perfectly well for applying a fitted model to new data, I often prefer another `broom` function: `augment()`. This returns a data frame that includes all relevant variables as well as the predicted values.

```{r}
# predictions only
predict(my_wf_fit, new_data = sol_test) 

# add preds and resids to df
sol_test_aug <- augment(my_wf_fit, new_data = sol_test) 
head(sol_test_aug)
```

This augmented data frame is particularly convenient when applying assessment functions like `yardstick::rmse()`

```{r}
rmse(sol_test_aug,
     truth = solubility,
     estimate = .pred)
```

On average, predictions made using this model miss true solubility by about .7 units.

## Bonus: plotting coefficient trajectories

It's often useful to visualize the trajectories of model coefficients as the penalty increases. Since `tune_grid()` doesn't retain model coefficients, some new code is needed.

```{r}
# desired penalty values for plot
lambda_vals <- 10^seq(-6, 1, length.out = 1000)

# model specification. penalty=1 is a placeholder ignored by glmnet()
lasso_spec2 <- linear_reg(mixture = 1, penalty = 1) |>  
  set_engine("glmnet", path_values = lambda_vals)

lasso_wf2 <- workflow(
  spec = lasso_spec2,
  preprocessor = my_rec
)

lasso_fit <-
  lasso_wf2 %>%
  fit(data = sol_train)
```

The output of `fit()` is an updated workflow object. In order to get model coefficients for each penalty value specified in `lambda_vals`, we use `extract_fit_engine` followed by `tidy()`.

```{r}
glmnet_object <- lasso_fit |> 
  extract_fit_engine()
coef_paths <- tidy(glmnet_object)
coef_paths
```

For neatness, let's restrict our plot to just a few interesting variables.

```{r}
vars <- c(
  "NumBonds",
  "NumAtoms",
  "HydrophilicFactor",
  "SurfaceArea1"
  )

coef_paths |> filter(term %in% vars) |> 
ggplot(aes(
    x = lambda, 
    y = estimate, 
    color = term)
    ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_segment(
    x = -6,
    y = 0,
    xend = 1, 
    linetype = "dotted"
    ) +
  labs(
    x = "Penalty",
    y = "Coefficient",
    color = "Variable"
    ) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) +
  scale_color_ee() + 
  theme_ee() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```
